interactions.label: Why do plain polysaccharide vaccines fail to protect infants under two years of

params.question: Why do plain polysaccharide vaccines fail to protect infants under two years of age?

answers.text: Maternal IgG crossing the placenta neutralises the polysaccharide before it can stimulate B cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Maternal IgG can interfere with some live vaccines, but this is not specific to polysaccharide antigens. The real issue is that polysaccharides cannot recruit T-cell help for class switching and memory.

answers.text: Polysaccharide antigens are T-independent, producing only IgM with no class switching or memory

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Polysaccharides stimulate B cells directly without T-cell help, generating mainly IgM with no memory. Conjugate vaccines link the polysaccharide to a carrier protein, converting it to a T-dependent antigen that activates the full adaptive pathway.

answers.text: Infants lack functional B lymphocytes during the first two years of life

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Infants possess functional B lymphocytes from birth. The limitation is not B-cell absence but the inability of polysaccharide antigens to engage T-cell help required for a mature immune response.

answers.text: The infant complement system cannot process polysaccharide antigens for presentation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complement can interact with polysaccharides, but antigen presentation depends on antigen-presenting cells, not complement. The failure lies in the T-independent nature of polysaccharide antigens.

overallFeedback.feedback: Polysaccharide antigens are T-independent: they stimulate B cells directly, yielding mainly IgM without class switching or memory. This is why conjugate vaccines, which link the polysaccharide to a carrier protein, are essential for protecting infants.

Exactly right. This is why conjugate vaccines like the Hib and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines were developed — they convert T-independent polysaccharides into T-dependent antigens that generate lasting memory even in young infants.

interactions.label: HIV infection primarily compromises humoral immunity by destroying B lymphocytes

params.question: HIV infection primarily compromises humoral immunity by destroying B lymphocytes, leading to susceptibility to opportunistic infections.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: HIV targets CD4+ T helper cells, not B lymphocytes. The collapse of cell-mediated immunity — not humoral immunity — is why HIV patients develop opportunistic infections caused by intracellular organisms that require Th1-driven macrophage activation for clearance.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. HIV selectively destroys CD4+ T helper cells, not B lymphocytes. The resulting collapse of cell-mediated immunity explains susceptibility to intracellular pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Pneumocystis jirovecii.

interactions.label: The Mantoux tuberculin skin test is positive in a patient previously exposed to

params.question: The Mantoux tuberculin skin test is positive in a patient previously exposed to Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Which component of the immune response does this test detect?

answers.text: Circulating IgG antibodies against mycobacterial cell wall antigens

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Mantoux test does not measure antibodies. It detects a cell-mediated response — specifically, Th1 memory cells that recognise tuberculin protein and recruit macrophages at the injection site.

answers.text: Complement-mediated lysis of tuberculin-coated cells at the injection site

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complement is not involved in the Mantoux response. The induration results from T-cell and macrophage infiltration, a hallmark of Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity.

The Mantoux test reads out Th1 memory. Previously sensitised CD4+ T cells recognise tuberculin, release interferon-gamma, and activate macrophages, producing visible induration at 48–72 hours — a classic Type IV hypersensitivity reaction.

answers.text: Natural killer cell cytotoxicity triggered by tuberculin protein

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Natural killer cells are part of innate immunity and do not generate antigen-specific memory. The Mantoux reaction is an adaptive, T-cell-mediated response that takes 48–72 hours to develop.

overallFeedback.feedback: The Mantoux test detects Th1-mediated delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV), not antibodies or complement. Sensitised CD4+ T cells recognise tuberculin protein and release interferon-gamma, activating macrophages and producing induration at 48–72 hours.

Well done. The Mantoux test is a clinical readout of Type IV hypersensitivity — sensitised Th1 cells recognise tuberculin and activate macrophages, producing the characteristic induration at 48–72 hours.

interactions.label: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus has a positive VDRL test but no clin

params.question: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus has a positive VDRL test but no clinical evidence of syphilis. What is the most likely explanation for this result?

answers.text: VDRL uses immunofluorescence that cross-reacts with antinuclear antibodies

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: VDRL is a flocculation test, not immunofluorescence. It detects anti-cardiolipin antibodies, which lupus patients produce as part of their autoimmune antibody profile.

answers.text: Complement consumption in lupus creates immune complexes that agglutinate the VDRL reagent

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While complement consumption occurs in lupus, it does not cause VDRL positivity. The false positive is specifically due to anti-cardiolipin antibodies that react with the cardiolipin in the VDRL reagent.

answers.text: VDRL becomes falsely positive in any patient receiving immunosuppressive therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Immunosuppressive therapy does not cause false-positive VDRL results. The false positivity arises from anti-cardiolipin antibodies that lupus patients produce independently of any treatment.

answers.text: Lupus patients produce anti-cardiolipin antibodies, and VDRL detects these rather than treponemal antibodies

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: VDRL is a non-treponemal test that detects antibodies against cardiolipin. SLE patients produce anti-cardiolipin antibodies as part of the antiphospholipid antibody syndrome. Always confirm syphilis with a treponemal-specific test such as FTA-ABS.

overallFeedback.feedback: VDRL is a non-treponemal screening test that detects anti-cardiolipin antibodies. Lupus patients produce these antibodies as part of their autoimmune profile, causing biological false positives. A treponemal-specific confirmatory test is always required.

Exactly right. VDRL detects anti-cardiolipin antibodies, not antibodies against Treponema pallidum. Since lupus patients produce anti-cardiolipin antibodies, a positive VDRL must always be confirmed with a treponemal-specific test.

interactions.label: A kidney transplant recipient develops graft failure within minutes of completin

params.question: A kidney transplant recipient develops graft failure within minutes of completing vascular anastomosis. Which immunological mechanism is most likely responsible?

answers.text: Preformed recipient antibodies binding donor HLA molecules on graft endothelium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes when preformed antibodies in the recipient bind donor HLA on graft endothelial cells, activating complement and causing widespread thrombosis. Pre-transplant crossmatch testing is performed specifically to prevent this.

answers.text: Direct recognition of donor MHC molecules by recipient T cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Direct T-cell recognition of donor MHC drives acute rejection, which takes days to weeks to develop — not minutes. The immediate timeline points to a pre-existing antibody-mediated process.

answers.text: Gradual fibrosis from processed donor peptides presented on recipient antigen-presenting cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes the indirect pathway of chronic rejection, which develops over months to years. The minutes-long timeline in this scenario is characteristic of antibody-mediated hyperacute rejection.

answers.text: Recipient natural killer cells lysing donor cells that lack self-MHC class I molecules

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: NK cell-mediated lysis of missing-self targets is relevant in bone marrow transplantation, not solid organ rejection within minutes. The immediate graft failure described here is caused by preformed antibodies triggering complement-mediated endothelial damage.

overallFeedback.feedback: Graft failure within minutes of vascular anastomosis indicates hyperacute rejection — caused by preformed recipient antibodies that bind donor HLA, activate complement, and trigger widespread endothelial thrombosis. This is prevented by pre-transplant crossmatch testing.

Correct. Hyperacute rejection is an antibody-mediated emergency occurring within minutes of transplantation. Preformed antibodies activate complement on graft endothelium, causing thrombosis and immediate graft loss. Pre-transplant crossmatching is the key preventive measure.
